name: Toussaint Louverture
role: General-in-chief and governor-general for life of Saint-Domingue (1797-1802)
summary: A formerly enslaved Catholic planter-steward who led the Haitian Revolution's black armies, ended slavery in Saint-Domingue and ruled it as a French colony almost independently. His 1801 constitution made him governor for life with near-absolute powers, made Catholicism the only public religion, tied cultivators to plantations under compulsory labor, censored the press and banned popular societies, while declaring all men free and equal before the law.

strong-leader.rationale: He made himself governor for life with sole initiative in lawmaking and appointment to all posts, and arrested or expelled French commissioners who obstructed him.

democracy-best.rationale: His constitution made him governor for life and let him choose his successor secretly, with no election of the executive and an assembly that meets in private for three months.

direct-votes.rationale: Laws are made only by a Central Assembly on the governor's proposal, elected indirectly, with no popular vote on laws.

elective-rulers.rationale: The constitution names him governor for life and gives him the sole right to choose his successor in a sealed packet.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The governor is named for life in the text itself and his successor is chosen secretly by him, not by popular election.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The constitution gives him the office for life and allows later governors to be continued every five years without limit.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Article 34 makes the governor commander in chief of the armed force, and Article 52 puts it at his disposition.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Central Assembly may only vote on laws the governor proposes, meets in private, and sits at most three months a year, while he promulgates and appoints to all offices.

separated-powers.rationale: The constitution gives courts life tenure and bars any authority from suspending their rulings, but the governor appoints to all posts, proposes all laws and organises the special tribunals.

term-limits.rationale: Assembly members may not serve more than six consecutive years, yet the governor holds office for life and later governors can be renewed without limit.

replace-appointed-officials.rationale: Municipal administrators are named for two years but may be continued, and judges keep office for life unless condemned.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: After the 1801 revolt he decreed deportation without trial, death for officers who failed to act, and forced labor in chains for seditious talk, while the constitution forbids arbitrary arrest.

party-controls-media.rationale: Article 39 has the governor oversee and censor, through commissioners, every writing meant for publication and suppress foreign ones.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He banned popular societies and seditious assemblies and ordered those whose statements trouble the order to be denounced and deported.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Article 67 bars any association contrary to public order and has seditious gatherings broken up by armed force.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Every person may petition the governor directly (Article 66) while popular societies are forbidden (Article 67).

decide-locally.rationale: Municipal officials are chosen by the governor from lists, limited to policing and records, and he fixes the territorial divisions himself.

leader-cult.rationale: The constitution itself names him governor for life in recognition of his glorious services and gives him a guard of honour paid by the colony.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Justice is administered by state first-instance, appeal and cassation tribunals created by the constitution.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Article 55 creates a colonial gendarmerie for policing countryside and towns.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The constitution sets up a paid and unpaid colonial guard and an army recruited under the governor.

state-harmful.rationale: He built a governing state with an executive, assembly, courts, police and army.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state he built maintains public worship, supervises schools and agriculture and directs labor, well beyond protection from violence.

taxation-theft.rationale: The constitution has the Assembly set taxes and lists customs duties and other levies as colonial revenue.

death-penalty.rationale: He decreed death for officers who refused legal orders in a revolt and gave special tribunals authority over murder, arson, rape and conspiracy.

revolution-justified.rationale: He joined the 1791 slave insurrection as its 'general doctor', helping plan the defence of its camp against the slaveowners' forces.

political-violence-never.rationale: He took part in the 1791 insurrection and arrested the French commissioner Roume and forced out Sonthonax and Hedouville to keep control of the colony.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: He had the French commissioner Roume seized by escort without any attack on him, and forced Sonthonax and Hedouville out of the colony.

traditional-family.rationale: The constitution protects marriage as the basis of morals, bans divorce and calls each plantation a family, and his decree calls marriage the most holy institution.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Article 10 provides that divorce will not take place in the colony.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The constitution gives marriage civil and religious institution and special government protection for married spouses.

civil-marriage.rationale: Marriage is described as a civil and religious institution, with municipal administrations keeping the registers of marriages.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: His decree dismisses officers who keep concubines or live with several women and treats marriage as the foundation of society.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: He ordered magistrates and generals to leave not a single woman living by libertinage in the cities and to send those without a trade to the fields.

more-religion-public.rationale: Catholicism is the only publicly professed religion, parishes pay for worship, and he called religion the basis of all virtues.

separate-church-state.rationale: The constitution makes Catholicism the only public faith, has each parish maintain its worship and ministers, and lets the governor assign ministers their spiritual scope.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The governor assigns each minister the scope of his spiritual administration and ministers may never form a body in the colony.

national-church-status.rationale: Article 6 allows only the Catholic religion to be publicly professed and Article 7 has the state-run parishes support it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He made Catholicism the sole public religion and called religion the foundation of virtue.

religion-illusion.rationale: He treated religion as the basis of all virtues and the foundation of social happiness and wrote the constitution's Catholic establishment.

harm-principle.rationale: His decrees punish idleness, concubinage and other private conduct, and the constitution bars divorce, none of which is justified by harm to others.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The constitution declares that every citizen owes services to the land, and his decrees tie cultivators to estates and require some task of everyone.

rule-by-example.rationale: Although he exhorts officers to set an example, his decrees rely on lists, security cards, prison terms, chain labor and the death penalty.

bound-labor.rationale: Article 16 and his proclamation fix cultivators on their estates, deny them passports and make fixing them 'immutable'.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: His decree sends idle Creoles to the fields, denies security cards to those without a trade and states that no one is exempt from some task.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: His decree says no one is exempt from some task, sends the idle and urban children to work on the estates and calls agriculture the most honourable state.

work-centre-of-life.rationale: He called idleness the source of all disorder and made labor the basis of freedom in the colony.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: His decree calls agriculture the most honourable state and blames city life for vice, vagabonds and prostitution, sending youth to the habitations.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Article 14 states that the colony cannot allow the least interruption of labor, and Article 67 bars associations contrary to public order.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Article 15 makes the owner or his representative the father of the habitation, with the governor enforcing mutual obligations and no voice for cultivators.

class-collaboration.rationale: Articles 15, 16 and 35 describe each estate as one family of owner and cultivators with a share of revenue, with the governor enforcing duties on both.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article 13 declares property sacred and inviolable and Article 73 returns sequestered estates to absentee owners who show title.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Article 13 declares property sacred and inviolable without making it depend on its use for the common good.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The constitution makes property sacred and restores seized estates to owners who present title.

land-redistribution.rationale: He returned estates to planters, restoring sequestered land to absentee owners on request, and tied cultivators to the estates.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: His regime ran on paid plantation labor: he declared that all labor deserves a salary and every salary demands work.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Article 18 prohibits importing goods of the same nature as the colony's own products.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: He opened trade with Britain and the United States, selling sugar for arms and goods.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Article 17 charges the governor to encourage the introduction of cultivators from abroad, and Article 60 lets foreigners hold goods in the colony.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Article 60 lets foreigners contract, acquire and receive goods situated in the colony and dispose of them like Frenchmen.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The constitution declares all men free, bars distinctions beyond virtue and talent and says the law is the same for all, though it binds cultivators to estates.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Article 4 opens all employment to every color and Article 5 makes the law the same for all.

racial-franchise.rationale: Article 5 admits no distinction but virtues and talents and the law is the same for all.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Article 5 says no distinction exists other than virtues and talents and no superiority except that granted by law in public office.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: In his memoir he says that when General Leclerc marched against him he resolved to defend himself with arms and would fight to the last.

notes: Positions are taken from his 1801 constitution and decrees, his record (arrests of commissioners, the 1791 insurrection) and his memoir. Searched themes: government, religion, family, labor, property, trade, justice, press, force; the economy, world affairs, technology and ecology have no statements of his in the sources. The 1801 constitution was drafted by an assembly he convened and is treated as his own because he approved and enforced it and called its drafting his work.
